faq.q: What is the difference between the v4 and v7 UUIDs it generates?
faq.a: v4 is 122 bits of cryptographic randomness with the version nibble fixed to 4 and the variant bits to 10 — ideal when you only need uniqueness and no ordering. v7 (RFC 9562) starts with a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp, then the version 7 and variant 10 bits, then random data, so a lexicographic sort of v7 UUIDs matches creation order. That ordering makes v7 far friendlier as a database primary key because new rows cluster at the end of the index instead of scattering like v4.

faq.q: Where does the randomness come from — is it secure?
faq.a: v4 uses the browser's native crypto.randomUUID() when present, and otherwise falls back to crypto.getRandomValues() with the version and variant bits set correctly by hand. v7 always fills its random portion from crypto.getRandomValues(). Both draw on the browser's cryptographically secure random generator, not Math.random(), and everything happens locally in the page.

faq.q: If I generate a bulk batch, do the v7 UUIDs stay in order?
faq.a: Yes. Many v7 UUIDs in a batch are created within the same millisecond, which would otherwise leave their order to chance. This tool keeps a per-millisecond counter in the 12 'rand_a' bits, so UUIDs minted in the same millisecond increment that counter and therefore sort in the exact order they were generated. You can generate from 1 to 1000 at once.

faq.q: What does the validator tell me, and does it decode v7 timestamps?
faq.a: Paste any UUID — in standard, uppercase, hyphen-free, brace or urn:uuid form — and it reports whether the string is well-formed (32 hex digits in the 8-4-4-4-12 layout), its version nibble and its variant bits. It specially recognises the nil UUID (all zeros) and the max UUID (all ones). For a v7 UUID it reads the 48-bit timestamp back out and shows it both as milliseconds since the epoch and as a decoded UTC and local date.
